articles.title: A forgotten 30-year forest experiment just delivered a huge surprise
articles.summary: A 30-year forestry experiment in Australia found that heavily thinned mountain ash forests grew unusually large trees while recovering enough carbon to match or exceed untouched areas. The results suggest carefully managed thinning could support timber production, wildlife habitat, and carbon storage at the same time.
articles.content:
What’s the best way to manage a forest? Australians have argued about this for decades. The debate is often framed as binary: do we protect forests entirely, or harvest trees to support local economies and communities?

The reality is more interesting, as our new research on a long-forgotten experiment in Victoria’s mountain ash forests reveals.

Since the 1970s, scientists and the public have questioned the use of clearfell logging – where all trees in a block of forest are cut down. Conservationists argued it destroys habitat for rare species and reduces the forests’ ecological value. Foresters said mountain ash is adapted to catastrophic bushfires, and clearfelling is the forestry equivalent.

The argument was heated and the polarization unhelpful. But the underlying questions about the impacts of clearfelling, and how they compared to less intensive forestry options, remained unresolved.

A landmark experiment

In the mid-1980s, the Victorian government launched a major restructure of the timber industry, and invested today’s equivalent of A$26 million to explore alternatives to clearfelling. This would use silviculture, the branch of forestry that deals with establishing, growing and tending forests.

The Silvicultural Systems Project was established at two sites between 1987 and 1989: Tanjil Bren in Victoria’s Central Highlands, and Cabbage Tree Creek in East Gippsland.

It was a landmark experiment, comparing forest regeneration across the full range of silvicultural approaches. These included traditional clearfells (250–350 meters wide), small patch clearfells (50–140 meters wide), and heavy thinnings, where 50–70% of trees were cut. Extensive areas of unharvested forest were kept as benchmarks for comparison.

The forest at Tanjil Bren was dense mountain ash regrowth from the 1939 fires. Hundreds of survey plots were established and thousands of seedlings were monitored. By the early 2000s, the results were clear: mountain ash regenerated best on clearfell sites. Where tall canopy trees were retained or the cleared patches were small, common understory species such as acacia dominated.

The findings were published. The access road grew over. The project sign collapsed. The experiment was forgotten. The debates continued.

But the trees kept growing.

Astounding results

In 2014 we visited the Tanjil Bren site as part of a University of Melbourne subject on silviculture in native forests. A colleague, Simon Murphy, had been involved in its establishment and suggested our students see the long-term outcomes of different silvicultural systems side-by-side. What we found was astounding.

The original results still held: 30 years later, the mountain ash in the large cleared patches and clearfelled areas was vigorous and abundant. But it was the heavily thinned parts of the forest that really caught our attention.

The trees left behind after thinning were enormous. While they were only 80 years old, the largest averaged well over a meter in diameter at chest height, and some were more than 1.5m. Thinning had given these trees more space and resources to grow, and they had responded dramatically. The largest trees in the thinned stands were 20% bigger in diameter than those in the unharvested control areas.

More remarkable still: the thinned stands of trees had stored as much or more carbon in their wood than the unharvested control areas. In just 30 years, the heavily thinned forest had not only recovered all the carbon removed during harvesting, but had also gained enough additional carbon to equal the increase seen in the unharvested controls.

These findings have profound implications. Bigger trees are more resistant to fires, so when the next fire occurs, they are more likely to survive. Bigger trees are also more likely to form hollows – a critical and declining habitat for rare species such as the greater glider and Leadbeater’s possum.

The acacia trees that grew in most of the silvicultural treatments are also vital for Leadbeater’s possums, which use it to forage and move around the forest. Camera traps across the sites confirmed this: Leadbeater’s possums were found in every silvicultural treatment plot we surveyed – but none of the unharvested areas.

Lessons for the future

The Tanjil Bren SSP offers three important lessons.

First, long-term silvicultural experiments are irreplaceable. Australia’s forests contain many forgotten experiments that could transform our understanding of how forests respond to human intervention. But all too often, they end up neglected, unfunded and forgotten. We should find them before it is too late.

Second, forest thinning is not a trade-off. Our findings show this for mountain ash, and other studies in North America have shown this for conifer forests. It can deliver wood for local industry, absorb carbon and improve habitat for wildlife. It is a win-win-win outcome that challenges the false dichotomy of conservation versus production that has dominated public debate for decades.

While thinning cannot (and should not) be done everywhere, it may be a useful tool to create more variety in tree ages and sizes, particularly in forests impacted by clearfelling or high-severity fire.

Third, and perhaps most importantly: there is no silvicultural silver bullet for managing forests. The long-forgotten experiment at Tanjil Bren has taught us that there are options available for managing our forests beyond clearfelling that can contribute to the societal demand for wood, maintain carbon stocks, and conserve biodiversity.

This discovery challenges the long-standing binary debate on forest management and offers a sustainable approach with broad environmental and societal benefits. The story is well-detailed, focuses on one main topic, and highlights a meaningful breakthrough with large-scale implications for forest conservation and climate action.
articles.personality_title: 30-year forest study shows thinning helps trees grow big and store carbon
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For many years, people in Australia have debated how best to manage forests. Some want to protect forests completely, while others support cutting trees to help local communities. A big question has been whether cutting all trees in an area (clearfell logging) or using gentler methods is better for the forest.

**What happened** – In the 1980s, the Victorian government started a large experiment in mountain ash forests to test different ways of managing trees. They tried clearfelling, small patch clearfelling, and heavy thinning (cutting 50-70% of trees). After 30 years, researchers returned to study the results. They found that trees in heavily thinned areas grew much larger than those in untouched forests. Surprisingly, these thinned forests stored as much or more carbon than untouched ones.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it shows thinning can help trees grow bigger and store carbon, while still allowing wood to be harvested. Bigger trees are better at surviving fires and provide homes for animals like the Leadbeater’s possum. This breaks the old idea that we must choose between protecting forests or using them for wood.

**What's next step** – Researchers suggest looking for other long-term forest experiments to learn more. They also believe thinning could be used more wisely to help forests recover after fires or logging. However, thinning is not a perfect solution for every forest and should be part of a mix of methods.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A 30-year study in Australian forests shows that carefully thinning trees can support bigger trees, wildlife, and carbon storage all at once.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:

articles.personality_title_es: Un estudio de 30 años muestra que el aclareo ayuda a crecer árboles grandes y almacenar carbono
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Australia, ha habido un debate largo sobre cómo manejar mejor los bosques. Algunas personas quieren protegerlos completamente, mientras que otras apoyan cortar árboles para ayudar a las comunidades locales. La pregunta era si era mejor cortar todos los árboles en un área (corte total) o usar métodos más suaves.

**Qué pasó** – En los años 80, el gobierno de Victoria inició un gran experimento en bosques de fresno de montaña para probar diferentes formas de manejar los árboles. Probaron el corte total, cortes en pequeñas áreas y aclareo fuerte (cortar entre el 50 y 70% de los árboles). Después de 30 años, los científicos regresaron a estudiar los resultados. Descubrieron que los árboles en las áreas aclaradas crecieron mucho más grandes que en los bosques sin tocar. Además, estos bosques aclarados almacenaron tanto o más carbono que los bosques sin cortar.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque muestra que el aclareo puede ayudar a que los árboles crezcan más grandes y almacenen carbono, mientras se permite la cosecha de madera. Los árboles grandes resisten mejor los incendios y ofrecen hogares para animales como el planeador de Leadbeater. Esto rompe la idea antigua de que hay que elegir entre proteger los bosques o usarlos.

**Próximos pasos** – Los investigadores sugieren buscar otros experimentos forestales a largo plazo para aprender más. También creen que el aclareo podría usarse mejor para ayudar a los bosques después de incendios o cortes. Pero el aclareo no es una solución para todos los bosques y debe usarse junto con otros métodos.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Un estudio de 30 años en bosques australianos muestra que aclarar árboles cuidadosamente puede apoyar árboles más grandes, la vida silvestre y el almacenamiento de carbono al mismo tiempo.

articles.title: Scientists just found a new way to make hydrogen from water
articles.summary: A new light-activated material can efficiently produce hydrogen from water without requiring an additional expensive metal catalyst. Researchers say its unusual sulfur-based chemistry could point toward cheaper and more practical ways to turn sunlight into clean fuel.
articles.content:
Researchers at Oregon State University have created a new class of materials that can use light to produce hydrogen from water, offering a potentially cleaner way to convert solar energy into fuel.

The work was led by Kyriakos Stylianou of the OSU College of Science. His team developed a photocatalyst capable of producing hydrogen quickly and efficiently. Hydrogen is widely used in fuel cells for vehicles, as well as in the production of ammonia, metal refining, and plastics manufacturing.

Using Light To Speed Up Chemical Reactions

A catalyst is a substance that accelerates a chemical reaction without being permanently changed in the process, Stylianou said. A photocatalyst works in a similar way but is activated by light. After absorbing light, the material reaches a higher energy state and can use that energy to drive chemical reactions more rapidly.

The findings, published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, could provide researchers with another tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and addressing climate change, Stylianou said.

His research centers on metal organic frameworks, or MOFs, which are crystalline, porous materials with structures that can be carefully customized.

MOFs are built from positively charged metal ions surrounded by organic "linker" molecules. Their tiny pores and adjustable structures allow scientists to fine tune their properties for different applications.

Millions of different MOF structures are theoretically possible, Stylianou said. Chemistry researchers have already synthesized nearly 100,000 of them, while the properties of roughly another half-million have been predicted.

An Unusual Sulfur Bond Drives the Reaction

For this study, the researchers focused on a MOF called BVR-19. The material contains an unusual sulfide-to-sulfide bond that temporarily breaks when exposed to light, producing highly reactive sulfur species.

"The organic component does the important work," Stylianou said. "Instead of relying primarily on the metal atoms, our material uses its sulfur-containing organic building blocks to capture light energy and move electrons where they are needed to produce hydrogen. This represents a different way of thinking about how these materials should be designed."

That approach means BVR-19 does not require an additional expensive metal catalyst, Stylianou added. This could make future light-driven hydrogen-production systems simpler to design.

The material also has another potential advantage. BVR-19 forms spontaneously in aqueous solutions at room temperature, which lowers the amount of energy required to make it.

A Cleaner Alternative to Conventional Hydrogen

Producing hydrogen by splitting water with a catalyst can be cleaner than the dominant industrial method, which relies on natural gas.

That conventional process, known as methane-steam reforming, releases carbon dioxide while producing hydrogen.

Existing methods for making hydrogen from water often rely on electrocatalysis, which uses electricity to drive the catalytic reaction. The environmental benefits of that approach depend heavily on where the electricity comes from. To remain both sustainable and economically competitive, the power must come from low-cost renewable sources.

At present, hydrogen produced through methane-steam reforming costs about $1.50 per kilogram, while green hydrogen costs roughly $5 per kilogram.

New Design Rules for Cheaper Green Hydrogen

"Our work provides a blueprint for designing better materials that can bring down the cost of green hydrogen," said Stylianou, who directs OSU's Materials Discovery Laboratory, known as the MaD Lab. "By changing the metal while keeping the rest of the material essentially the same, we discovered why some versions of the MOF work much better than others. These findings provide new design rules for creating more effective materials for solar fuel production."

MaD Lab members Emmanuel Musa, Dylan Pyle, Jacob Lessard, Andrzej Gladysiak, Ankit Yadav, Silas Blessed and Prayash Mohanty were joined in the research by Oregon State's Logan Lancaster, Taylor Krueger, Min Soo Jung, Galen Fritz, Jacob Hirschi, Hongliang Huang, William Stickle, Xiulei "David" Ji, Chong Fang and Tim Zuehlsdorff.

The Murdock Charitable Trust, the National Science Foundation and the OSU College of Science supported the study.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos desarrollan nuevo material activado por luz para producir hidrógeno a partir del agua
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El hidrógeno es un combustible limpio importante usado en vehículos e industria, pero producirlo de forma ecológica y económica sigue siendo un desafío. Hoy en día, la mayoría del hidrógeno se fabrica a partir de gas natural, lo que libera dióxido de carbono y daña el medio ambiente.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad Estatal de Oregón crearon un nuevo material llamado BVR-19 que usa la luz para separar el agua y producir hidrógeno. Este material funciona sin necesidad de metales caros y se basa en una química especial con azufre. Se forma fácilmente en agua a temperatura ambiente, lo que lo hace más simple y barato de producir.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento ofrece un nuevo método para producir hidrógeno verde que podría ser más barato y práctico que las opciones actuales. Como no usa metales costosos y aprovecha la luz solar directamente, podría ayudar a reducir la contaminación relacionada con la producción de hidrógeno. Esto podría hacer que el hidrógeno limpio sea más accesible para pilas de combustible e industria.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo de investigación planea explorar otros materiales similares cambiando sus partes metálicas para encontrar versiones mejores. Esperan mejorar la eficiencia y reducir el costo de la producción solar de hidrógeno, acercándose a aplicaciones reales.

**Una frase clave** – Un nuevo material activado por luz con química de azufre podría permitir hidrógeno más barato y limpio producido directamente del agua y la luz solar.

articles.title: Two years after Hurricane Helene, survivors are taking lessons for the future
articles.content:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and BPR, a public radio station serving western North Carolina. ​

In the days and weeks after Hurricane Helene, people throughout western North Carolina and beyond found themselves thrust into new situations, forced to learn new skills to help themselves and their neighbors.

Community centers, churches, and fire departments flung open their doors, and for months, they buzzed with activity. Stacks of clothes covered altars. Tools and equipment filled spare rooms. Residents learned how to strip homes to the studs and built networks for bringing food, water, and other essential supplies to one another.

Now, two years later, people want to turn these ad hoc efforts — which supported communities through the loss of power, water, internet, and other crucial services — into more permanent fixtures of local disaster response, called “resilience hubs.”

“It’s become one of those terms, I think, that sometimes feels a little nebulous to people,” McKenzie Jones, a director with Urban Sustainability Directors Network, said. “But resilience hubs are just existing community spaces that are used and trusted by residents.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The East Asheville Library, for instance, is installing solar panels. At the Asheville Tool Library, people are learning how to wield power tools. And at the Old Fort Train Depot, locals recently discussed a heat wave action plan during an ice cream social.

The city is stepping up as well. Earlier this year, Asheville set aside $2 million to shore up the city’s existing hubs. City Manager D.K. Wesley made a soft commitment of spending up to $10 million over the long term.

This effort reflects a broader movement, as communities across the country invest in resilience hubs to prepare for power outages, extreme weather and other emergencies. But Helene also showed that resilience doesn’t necessarily require a designated hub. It can reside in the skills, equipment, and connections people can draw on even before the next disaster arrives.

“So the question is, How do we get them all to work together proactively before something happens and build those networks so that when it does happen, they’re able to support each other more effectively?” Jones said.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Two years after Helene, those lessons are taking root across western North Carolina. Here are four ways communities are turning what they learned in the disaster and its aftermath into tools for whatever comes next.

The solar installation at Beacon of Hope took a little over a week. Electricians who worked on the project say demand for solar has been high since the storm. Katie Myers / Grist / Blue Ridge Public Radio

Keeping the lights on with solar power

On a sunny morning in Marshall, Steve Porvaznik and Ryan Callahan, both electricians with Rhino Renewables, put the final touches on a solar installation. They secured white covers over three batteries, each about 3 feet tall and containing a nest of wires and conductors.

The work capped a week spent outfitting Beacon of Hope, a laundromat, thrift store, and food bank with the equipment needed to create a microgrid. “We were able to back up the whole store, essentially, with all the freezers and coolers,” Porvaznik said. The batteries can store an estimated 68 kilowatt-hours of solar power, allowing Beacon to keep the lights and appliances running for at least a day without sunlight or a connection to the larger electrical grid.

It is the first of 26 microgrids planned for western North Carolina. Twenty-four will serve community centers, food banks, fire departments, and other essential facilities. Two more will be mounted on trailers and sent wherever they are needed. A $5 million grant from the state Department of Environmental Quality is funding the work.

At Beacon of Hope, keeping the power on means the freezers, washing machines, and other equipment continue running. Director Jessi Koontz said the food pantry provides weekly food assistance to about 1,600 families, with hunger up about 50 percent since last summer.

“People already come here,” she said. “So, how can we maximize the resources that are available and the communication that is available when they come here?”

Jessi Koontz runs Beacon of Hope, a food pantry, thrift store, and community laundromat in Marshall, North Carolina. Katie Myers / Grist / Blue Ridge Public Radio

Those leading the microgrid campaign hope to expand beyond the 26 already in the works, but so far neither state nor federal officials have provided additional funding. That’s a common impediment to expanding such programs, said Alex Kwasinski, a University of Pittsburgh engineer who studies microgrids and disasters.

Sarah Nichols of Land of Sky, one of the organizations bringing the technology to the region, is working to identify more community hubs that would benefit from solar microgrids. The best locations sit on high ground and serve populations with high needs.

“Are we looking at equity?” Nichols said. “Should we put it in a more rural area or in a community that might not traditionally get access to government services?”

During an outage as widespread as Helene’s, such hubs could keep food and medication cold and communications running while providing a safe, warm, and dry place for people whose homes have lost power.

– Katie Myers

Justin Hamel of WNC Radio Project tunes into a Saturday night net hosted by a repeater in Fletcher. Laura Hackett / Blue Ridge Public Radio

Staying connected when cell networks go down

Every Saturday night, William Walker has a standing appointment with his two-way radio. The retired railroad worker runs a weekly check-in, called a “net,” from his home in Fletcher, connecting with dozens of radio enthusiasts who have turned a hobby into a public service.

Over a crackly signal, regulars check in from as far away as South Carolina, sharing snippets about their lives: a 41st birthday, a granddaughter’s wedding, an afternoon spent chopping wood. These exchanges go on for about half an hour, with Walker as master of ceremonies.

“It’s kind of like having family come into your living room every Saturday night,” he said. “We’ve tried to make it a very welcoming place. I mean, if there was ever a bunch that’s never been a stranger, it’s the people that I’ve met on the GMRS radio.”

A repeater stationed high up in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Adam Trescott

GMRS, or general mobile radio service, is a two-way system that doesn’t need a cell network or internet connection. A license costs $35 and there is no test, making it easy for anyone to participate. Walker’s weekly check-ins allow people to “overcome their mic fright” and make sure their equipment works.

That preparation gained urgency after Helene knocked out communication across a wide swath of the region, leaving people cut off from loved ones and vital information. The number of licenses jumped by 130 percent in the year after the storm.

Fairview resident Justin Hamel saw the value of GMRS firsthand. “We were really struggling to connect,” he said. He eventually got his hands on some “bubble radios,” as walkie-talkies with GMRS capabilities are known, and passed them out to neighbors.

It wasn’t perfect, and mountain ridges occasionally blocked signals, but everyone could share updates about water, supplies, and cleanup efforts. Hamel even helped relay information to first responders who dispatched a helicopter for a medical emergency.

Inspired by the experience, Hamel launched WNC Radio Project, a nonprofit that teaches people about the technology and works to expand its reach by installing small devices called signal repeaters on mountaintops. “With the aid of repeaters, you can talk across multiple counties,” he said. “Basically, think like a cell phone tower.”

He’s already installed two of them, and the network allowed him to communicate with neighbors during Winter Storm Fern and other severe weather — exactly the situation it was built for. “Radio’s superpower is that it enables instantaneous ad hoc group communication,” Hamel said. “All you have to do is pick up your radio, turn it on, and hit that button.”

– Laura Hackett

Shelby Treichler is the operations coordinator at the Asheville Tool Library, a site where people can rent out and train on power tools. Laura Hackett / Blue Ridge Public Radio

Equipping a new wave of power tool users

The day after Hurricane Helene made landfall, Shelby Treichler was determined to make it to the Asheville Tool Library. The power was out and she knew the library, where she is an operations coordinator, had a solar panel setup that would be crucial in the days ahead.

There was just one problem: A fallen tree blocked the only road out of her neighborhood.

“I didn’t think to bring my tools home with me. None of us thought to be on that level prepared,” she said. Armed with only a handsaw, she started cutting, hoping to at least clear a lane. Then, seemingly out of nowhere, a man wearing sandals arrived with a chainsaw. He jumped from his truck and started bucking the tree. A few minutes later, he drove off, leaving Treichler in tears.

“I was like, ‘This is community. This is beautiful,’” she said. “The guy just got back in the truck and drove away. We all barely exchanged three words except for, ‘This is crazy, huh?’”

Treichler’s experience was repeated across western North Carolina in the days after Helene. Unofficial chainsaw brigades, composed largely of volunteers, fanned out to clear roads. Appalachian poet Gerald Smith described hearing “the sweet, sweet sound of chainsaws,” a familiar refrain that inspired a new wave of people to learn how to use one.

A chainsaw safety workshop held by N.C. State and Skills Academy for Women in late 2024. Quetzal Jordan

Quetzal Jordan, founder of Skills Academy for Women, is among those showing them how. She has led more than 500 people through safety workshops since Helene. “I’ve taught people anywhere from 18 to 75 how to use a chainsaw,” she said. “And especially the folks who are older, I feel like they have the most transformative experience.”

The chainsaw classes are part of a broader movement in western North Carolina to treat tools and the skills to use them as a form of climate resilience. The Asheville Tool Library, for instance, lends everything from saws and shovels to generators and megaphones and teaches people how to use them. Insurance prevents it from lending chainsaws, but it keeps several among its collection of more than 4,000 tools for emergencies.

“We were doing this work before and resiliency was kind of in all of our minds, but I think, like most people who are affected by Hurricane Helene, it’s taken on a very different meaning now and a very different sense of urgency,” Treichler said.

– Laura Hackett

Swannanoa Communities Together serves Swannanoa residents, many of whom have unique medical vulnerabilities and language needs. Katie Myers / Grist / Blue Ridge Public Radio

Making emergency planning more inclusive

Walter Davis, 67, has multiple disabilities and can’t drive. He takes several medications, and a work injury left him without the use of one foot. When Helene hit his apartment complex in Swannanoa, he relied on neighbors for help.

“For about three and a half weeks we had no power, no water,” he said while waiting for the bus one day last month. “We had to go down to the creek and get five-gallon buckets of water and flush our toilets with it.”

The storm also took out the only grocery store within walking distance, and many of his neighbors don’t drive.

These challenges extend far beyond Swannanoa. Census data released in 2023 show that while about 1 percent of U.S. adults had been displaced by a disaster in the previous year, the figure rose to 31 percent among those unable to care for themselves. Many people with disabilities never returned home after evacuating, and more than 74 percent of evacuees unable to walk reported experiencing food insecurity a month after a disaster.

State agencies coordinate with emergency services to get information out, but local officials aren’t always aware of the scale of need in an emergency. “Disabled folks are typically not at the table when planning for emergency response,” said Dom Kelly, the founder and director of the advocacy group New Disabled South.

Malia Johnson has a cochlear implant and identifies as deaf. She struggled to keep up with accurate information after Hurricane Helene. Katie Myers / Grist / Blue Ridge Public Radio

Those gaps became apparent in Swannanoa after Helene. A friend living at Jasper Apartments asked Beth Trigg to help check on medically vulnerable residents, about 100 of whom had been unable to evacuate. She and other volunteers fanned out across that complex and others to ask what people needed and find essentials like insulin and bottled oxygen. “We really immediately saw the different needs of people who had specific medical issues or disabilities,” Trigg said.

That effort grew into Swannanoa Communities Together, which provides therapy and long-term support ranging from help navigating FEMA to rent assistance. The group operates out of a former hair salon and recently bought adjoining lots, with plans to renovate the building with ADA-compliant bathrooms, wheelchair ramps, and changing stations. An accessibility consultant is helping ensure the space can serve as many people as possible.

“We’re seeing it as a place where we can have emergency response for our community in future emergencies or future disasters,” Trigg said.

– Katie Myers

articles.personality_title: Western North Carolina builds stronger communities after Hurricane Helene
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Two years ago, Hurricane Helene caused widespread damage in western North Carolina. Many communities lost power, water, and communication, forcing residents to rely on each other for help. 

**What happened** – Since then, people and local groups have worked to turn emergency efforts into lasting solutions. They created “resilience hubs” in community centers, libraries, and fire stations where neighbors can gather during disasters. For example, a laundromat in Marshall was equipped with solar panels and batteries to keep running during power outages. Volunteers also set up radio networks to stay connected when cell phones fail. Workshops teach people how to safely use tools like chainsaws to clear debris. Groups are making emergency plans that include people with disabilities and other special needs.

**Impact** – These actions help communities prepare better for future storms and emergencies. Solar microgrids keep food and medicine cold even when the power goes out. Radio networks allow quick communication across wide areas without relying on cell towers. Teaching tool skills empowers more people to help with cleanup and repairs. Making emergency plans inclusive ensures that vulnerable residents are not left behind. This approach turns short-term crisis responses into ongoing support systems.

**What's next step** – The city of Asheville has committed millions of dollars to improve resilience hubs and expand solar microgrids. Local groups plan to build more communication repeaters on mountain tops and continue training workshops. Swannanoa Communities Together is renovating a building to better serve people during emergencies. These efforts aim to connect and strengthen communities before the next disaster strikes.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Western North Carolina is turning lessons from Hurricane Helene into lasting community networks, solar power projects, and inclusive emergency plans to better face future disasters.

articles.title: ‘He felt heard’: How a film brought a UN report to life in Xochimilco
articles.summary: A documentary drawn from United Nations University research was screened at the COP30 climate conference and film festivals across Europe. Its most important journey, though, was the one back to the Mexico City canals where it was filmed.
articles.content:
Scientific reports rarely leave the shelf. Sometimes, though, the research itself becomes a real story that sparks conversations far beyond academia.

That is what happened in Xochimilco, in Mexico City.

In 2025, the UN University Institute for Environment and Human Security (UNU-EHS) published a report on interconnected risks.

It asked why societies struggle to make the changes needed to tackle climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. One conclusion: societies must think beyond the short term and weigh the wellbeing of future generations.

To bring that idea to life, the researchers turned to Xochimilco. For centuries, its chinamperos have cultivated chinampas – fertile plots built on wetlands that produce food while preserving knowledge handed down through generations.

Today that living heritage faces urbanization, environmental degradation, climate change and a shifting relationship between young people and the land.

The result was a documentary, Chinamperos: Preserving Ancestral Farming Practices in Mexico City, directed by Mexican filmmaker Rodrigo Jardón Galeana and shot in San Gregorio Atlapulco.

The aim was simple – take a scientific report off the page and show what it means for people at the centre of it in real terms.

© UNU-EHS/Rodrigo Jardón Gal

A call that reverberated

Mariana Páez, one of those featured, shared the film on social media expecting family, friends and neighbours to watch. Instead, she also heard from people she had not spoken to in years.

Among them were Karen Ramírez and Abel Bastida, former schoolmates on different career paths who shared a fascination with the place where they grew up. A video call planned for 20 or 30 minutes ran to nearly two hours – farming, food, traditions, water, the problems they saw around them.

“We couldn’t stop talking,” Ms. Páez recalls.

That conversation led the three to found the Permanent Seminar on Xochimilco Studies, or SEPEX, to open up dialogue about the territory and its culture. A film meant to communicate research had sparked a local conversation nobody had seen coming.

Heard at last

The documentary has since been screened at COP30 in Brazil and at festivals in Spain, Greece, Türkiye and the Czech Republic. Our colleagues in the UN News Spanish team also told the chinamperos’ story in April 2025.

For Ms. Páez, though, the most important effects were closer to home. In her own family, the film brought greater recognition to work and Indigenous knowledge that had not always been valued like other professions.

One of those featured, chinampero Samuel Avelino, died earlier this year. Ms. Páez later discovered that a screenshot of the UN News story carrying his testimony was among the last things he shared on Facebook.

“He felt heard,” she says.

That matters, she explains, because the everyday lives of chinamperos rarely reach beyond their own circles. Outsiders rarely ask what a day working the land is like.

© UNU-EHS/Rodrigo Jardón Gal

Coming home

More than a year on, the film returned to Mexico. SEPEX helped organize a visit to Xochimilco for representatives of the University and the UN in Mexico, and screenings followed at the National Centre for the Arts and the Metropolitan Autonomous University.

Residents, researchers, students, UN staff and city officials came together. The aim was not just to show a film, but to let the community speak directly to researchers and decision makers.

“Xochimilco is a living territory,” said Allegra Baiocchi, the UN Resident Coordinator in Mexico – a place where biodiversity, water management, climate adaptation, food security and ancestral knowledge all converge.

For Shen Xiaomeng, Vice-Rector of the University in Europe and Director of UNU-EHS, the trip was a chance to give something back.

Meeting chinampero Eric Enríquez, she noted the pride with which he spoke about his work. Farmers’ survival, she said, depends on how much society values them – but everyone else depends on those who grow our food.

© UNU-EHS/Rodrigo Jardón Gal

A window, not a solution

Ms. Ramírez sees the film not as a solution but as a “window”. It’s a way of looking at what may lie ahead before deciding what to do. She wants it screened in more neighbourhoods and public spaces across Xochimilco, with children joining the conversations.

Mr. Bastida stresses that Xochimilco is not simply a landscape in need of preservation. People live there, with different needs and different visions of its future.

The documentary does not resolve those differences. But it has done something less visible, and perhaps necessary before any solution can emerge: created a place where people can meet on common ground and talk about them.

articles.personality_title_fr: Un documentaire donne vie à la recherche climatique dans les canaux de Xochimilco au Mexique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2025, l’Institut des Nations Unies pour l’environnement et la sécurité humaine (UNU-EHS) a publié un rapport sur les défis liés au changement climatique, à la pollution et à la perte de biodiversité. Le rapport souligne que les sociétés doivent penser aux générations futures pour résoudre ces problèmes.

Un agriculteur présenté dans le film s’est senti « écouté » avant de décéder, montrant que le documentaire a donné de la valeur à des vies quotidiennes rarement vues par les étrangers.

articles.personality_title_es: Un documental da vida a la investigación climática en los canales de Xochimilco, México
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2025, el Instituto de las Naciones Unidas para el Medio Ambiente y la Seguridad Humana (UNU-EHS) publicó un informe sobre los retos del cambio climático, la contaminación y la pérdida de biodiversidad. El informe dice que las sociedades deben pensar en las futuras generaciones para resolver estos problemas.

**Qué pasó** – Para mostrar esta idea, los investigadores trabajaron con chinamperos, agricultores en Xochimilco, Ciudad de México, que usan métodos antiguos para cultivar en tierras húmedas llamadas chinampas. Se hizo un documental llamado "Chinamperos: Preservando prácticas agrícolas ancestrales en Ciudad de México", dirigido por Rodrigo Jardón Galeana. Se presentó en la conferencia climática COP30 y en festivales en Europa, pero su mayor impacto fue en Xochimilco, donde reunió a la gente para hablar sobre su tierra y tradiciones.

**Impacto** – La película ayudó a iniciar nuevas conversaciones entre los locales, incluyendo amigos que se reencontraron y formaron un grupo llamado SEPEX para estudiar y proteger la cultura de Xochimilco. También dio más respeto al trabajo de los chinamperos y su conocimiento indígena, que a menudo pasa desapercibido. Un agricultor que apareció en el documental se sintió “escuchado” antes de fallecer, mostrando cómo la película valoró vidas cotidianas que rara vez ven los demás.

**Próximo paso** – El documental volvió a México para proyecciones comunitarias con residentes, estudiantes, investigadores y autoridades. La gente lo usa como una “ventana” para entender diferentes opiniones sobre el futuro de Xochimilco. Los organizadores quieren mostrarlo en más barrios y que los niños participen en las charlas, ayudando a crear un terreno común antes de buscar soluciones.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un documental basado en la investigación de la ONU ha inspirado conversaciones locales y globales sobre proteger la agricultura ancestral y el medio ambiente de Xochimilco, conectando a personas de todas las generaciones y culturas.
